newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Exxon faces weaker prices, but has big purse.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Exxon faces weaker prices, but has big purse.

text.p: A bumper second quarter from oil giant Exxon Corp drove the company's stock higher on Wall Street, but analysts say that the company will start to feel the impact of weaker oil prices in the second half.
Exxon closed up 14/16 at 61-5/16, somewhat off its day's best of 62-1/8 after the company announced a record second quarter on the back of stronger than expected refining and marketing profits.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Michael Young upgraded his 1997 EPS forecast by 10 cents to $3.15 after the results.
"It would be a mistake to extrapolate this downstream performance through the rest of the year," he said.

However, Exxon, the biggest profit-maker in the Fortune 500 in 1996, has the financial firepower to ensure that it can keep on growing dividends and increase share buybacks throughout this year thanks to its low debt to equity ratio.

In the second quarter, Exxon not only beat last year's earnings per share of $0.63 when it turned in $0.79 this year, but may be the only major international oil company based in the U.S. to turn in higher earnings than the first quarter.

U.S. refining and marketing earnings came in 62 percent ahead of forecasts of a flat year-on-year performance when they rose to $162 million from $98.0 million a year ago, and overseas, the company easily beat the $300 million expected from analysts with $382 million compared to $134 million a year ago.

"These results are quite spectacular, the company's refining and marketing division did very well, but where refining margins are in the second half is open to speculation," said Salomon Brothers analyst Paul Ting.
Where the company did suffer was in the upstream sector.

It cited a $1.50 per barrel decline in average realised oil prices from a year ago and an 18 cents per MCF decline in natural gas prices, and analysts say that in the second half the outlook is more bearish.

In the first quarter Exxon's upstream activities benefitted from a $3.00 per barrel rise in oil prices and for the first six months of 1997, that strength was also evident with better earnings from a year ago.
A $1.00 per barrel change in oil prices affects Exxon's earnings by around $0.12 per share and a $0.10 change in natural gas prices by $0.02 per share.
U.S. exploration and production earnings were $335 million, compared with $423 million in the second quarter last year, while outside the U.S. they were flat at $620 million.
"In the second half the macro-economic picture for the oil industry as a whole, not just Exxon, is looking worse," said Salomon's Ting.

He says that one positive for Exxon is the preponderance of specialty chemicals in its portfolio, which will mean the company is less vulnerable to any downturn in the bulk chemicals market than others.

Chemical earnings were $393 million, up $89 million from second quarter 1996 as sale volumes rose eight percent from the prior year and margins improved on the strengthening of commodity chemicals prices and lower feedstock costs.
Schroder & Co analyst Michael Mayer raised earnings per share forecasts for 1997 by $0.15 to reflect improved foreign downstream and chemicals earnings.
One area where Exxon has a key advantage over its peers is its low debt to capitalisation ratio, around 17 percent.

During the second quarter, the company repurchased 14.9 million shares for some $863 million and Mayer, while maintaining the stock as a market performer has a target price for the stock of $62.00 and upside potential to $68.00.

"Our target price reflects Exxon's unparalleled ability to grow its dividend and buy back stock, while maintaining an excellent balance sheet," he said. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
